title: THE TWO MEN WHO REFUSED TO FEAR THE GIANTS
paragraphs:
THE TWO MEN WHO REFUSED TO FEAR THE GIANTS
Twelve men saw the same giants. Ten came back terrified. Two came back believing. And the difference was never the size of the giants—it was the size of the God they believed was standing with them.
There are moments when fear does not knock politely.
It kicks the door open.
The diagnosis comes back.
The marriage starts breaking.
The bills pile higher than the money.
Someone you trusted becomes someone you barely recognize.
The temptation you thought you defeated returns.
The prayer you have prayed for months seems to disappear into silence.
And suddenly there is a giant standing between you and everything you thought God promised.
That is where Numbers 13 takes us.
Not into a comfortable Bible story.
Into a crisis of faith.
Israel had already watched God humiliate Egypt's idols, split the sea, drown Pharaoh's army, provide bread in the wilderness, and reveal His presence among His people.
They had evidence.
They had history.
They had promises.
And still, when twelve spies entered Canaan and returned forty days later, ten men essentially said:
We cannot do this.
The people are too strong.
The cities are too fortified.
The giants are too big.
And tragically, they were not lying about what they saw.
That is what makes this story so painfully relevant.
Faith is not pretending the giants are small.
Biblical faith does not require you to lie about your cancer.
It does not require you to pretend betrayal did not hurt.
It does not demand that you call financial devastation "nothing."
It does not tell a grieving mother to stop crying.
It does not ask the exhausted Christian to pretend everything is wonderful.
The ten spies saw real obstacles.
Joshua and Caleb saw them too.
The difference was not eyesight.
The difference was interpretation.
Ten interpreted the giants without adequately accounting for God.
Two interpreted the giants in light of God.
And somebody reading this needs to understand the difference.
Numbers 13:30 tells us that Caleb quieted the people before Moses and declared:
“Let us go up at once and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.”
The Hebrew carries an intensity that English can easily flatten:
עָלֹה נַעֲלֶה
ʿālōh naʿăleh
The construction intensifies the verbal idea.
We can capture its force approximately as:
“We should absolutely go up.”
Then Caleb says:
יָכוֹל נוּכַל לָהּ
yākhol nūkhal lāh
Again, the Hebrew intensifies the declaration:
“We are certainly able to overcome it.”
Caleb was not practicing positive thinking.
He was not standing in front of a mirror repeating affirmations about his own greatness.
His confidence was rooted in something infinitely greater than self-confidence.
God had spoken.
That changes everything.
But the other spies looked at the same land and said:
“We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.”
Then came one of Scripture's most haunting descriptions of fear.
They said they saw the Nephilim, and then confessed:
וַנְּהִי בְעֵינֵינוּ כַּחֲגָבִים
vannehi veʿeineinu kaḥagavim
“We were in our own eyes like grasshoppers.”
Read those words again.
“In our own eyes.”
Before the giants defeated Israel on a battlefield, fear had already reduced these men inside their own minds.
They had become grasshoppers to themselves.
And fear still does this.
It whispers:
You are too damaged.
Too ordinary.
Too weak.
Too late.
Too sinful.
Too far gone.
Your family will never change.
Your addiction will always own you.
Your past will always define you.
Your failure is bigger than your future.
Your shame has the final word.
And sometimes the most dangerous giant is not standing in front of you.
It is speaking inside you.
The ten spies spread their fear through the camp.
That is another uncomfortable truth.
Fear is contagious.
One frightened voice became ten.
Ten frightened voices became a nation crying through the night.
People began wishing they had died in Egypt.
Some even wanted another leader who would take them back.
Back.
To Egypt.
Back to bondage.
Back to the place God had delivered them from.
Fear can make slavery look safer than obedience.
Sit with that.
Because some of us have done the same thing.
God begins pulling us out of something destructive, but when obedience becomes frightening, suddenly the old chains begin looking familiar.
You start missing the relationship God rescued you from.
You romanticize the addiction that was destroying you.
You reconsider the compromise you once begged God to break.
You return mentally to Egypt because Canaan contains giants.
But Joshua and Caleb refused to join the panic.
Numbers 14 tells us that Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh tore their clothes.
They pleaded with the people.
The land was exceedingly good.
If the LORD delighted in them, He would bring them into it.
Then they said:
“Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land.”
And then comes an astonishing declaration:
יְהוָה אִתָּנוּ אַל־תִּירָאֻם
YHWH ʾittānu, ʾal-tirāʾum.
“The LORD is with us. Do not fear them.”
There it is.
The entire battle compressed into one sentence.
The LORD is with us.
Joshua and Caleb were not fearless because the giants had disappeared.
They refused to be ruled by fear because God's presence mattered more than the giants' size.
That is biblical courage.
Courage is not the absence of trembling.
Courage is obedience when trembling has not stopped.
Faith is not saying, “There is no giant.”
Faith says, “There is a giant—and there is God.”
And God is not the smaller reality.
But we must be careful here.
This passage is not a blank check promising Christians that every personal dream will succeed if they simply believe hard enough.
Canaan was connected to a specific covenant promise God had given Israel.
So we should not turn Joshua and Caleb into mascots for self-help spirituality.
“Believe in yourself and conquer your dreams” is not the Gospel.
The deeper biblical principle is far more demanding:
Trust God enough to obey Him even when obedience frightens you.
And that brings us somewhere even deeper.
Because Joshua's name matters.
In Hebrew, Joshua is יְהוֹשֻׁעַ — Yehoshua.
The Greek form associated with that name is Ἰησοῦς — Iēsous.
Jesus bears that name.
And while Joshua son of Nun is not Jesus Christ, the biblical storyline ultimately carries us beyond Joshua and beyond Canaan toward the greater Deliverer.
Joshua led Israel toward earthly inheritance.
Jesus came to rescue sinners from enemies no human warrior could conquer.
Sin.
Condemnation.
Death.
We spend so much time talking about the giants around us that we can miss the monster within us.
The greatest human problem is not that life is difficult.
It is that humanity is alienated from a holy God by sin.
We do not merely need improved circumstances.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need new hearts.
We need Jesus.
And this is where the Gospel becomes scandalously beautiful.
Jesus did not come for people who had successfully defeated every giant.
He came for sinners.
For failures.
For deniers.
For doubters.
For people carrying histories they wish they could erase.
For people who promised God, “Never again,” and then did it again.
For people who know exactly how Peter must have felt when the rooster crowed.
For people who cannot believe God would still want them after everything they have done.
The cross answers that fear.
Christ did not die because humanity had finally become worthy of Him.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Grace walked toward the guilty.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
That means your sin is serious—but for everyone who comes to Christ in repentance and faith, your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Your shame does not own the pen.
Your worst night does not own the pen.
Your addiction does not own the pen.
Your divorce does not own the pen.
Your betrayal does not own the pen.
Your failure does not own the pen.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your giant tonight has a name.
Maybe nobody knows it.
You smile at church.
You post encouraging verses.
You tell people you are blessed.
But behind the closed door, you are tired.
You have been fighting thoughts you are ashamed to admit.
You have wondered whether God has become tired of you.
You have asked whether you have failed too many times.
Maybe you have been staring at your giant so long that you have started seeing yourself as a grasshopper.
Small.
Powerless.
Finished.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not discovering that you are secretly powerful enough.
The answer is discovering again who Christ is.
Paul did not say, “I can survive because I finally discovered how impressive I am.”
His confidence was in Christ.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of strong people accomplishing impossible things for God.
It is the story of weak people discovering that God's grace is sufficient.
That changes the way we face giants.
Sometimes God removes the giant.
Sometimes He takes you through the battle.
Sometimes the prayer is answered differently than you desperately hoped.
Some believers are healed.
Others glorify Christ while suffering.
Some doors open.
Others remain closed.
Some storms stop.
In others, Christ keeps His people while the storm continues.
Faith does not dictate to God how the story must unfold.
Faith trusts the Author when we cannot understand the chapter.
Joshua and Caleb did not control the outcome.
They trusted the One who did.
And perhaps that is where this story has found you.
Standing between promise and fear.
Between yesterday's evidence of God's faithfulness and tomorrow's terrifying uncertainty.
You know what Scripture says.
You know what Christ has done.
But the giant still looks enormous.
Then do what Joshua and Caleb did.
Look again.
Not away from reality.
Look beyond it.
There is something bigger than the giant.
There is Someone.
Jesus Christ.
The One who touched lepers when others backed away.
The One who welcomed sinners when religious people wanted distance.
The One who forgave the undeserving.
The One who stood before death itself.
The One who entered a grave.
The One who walked out.
And because He lives, hopelessness does not get automatic authority over your story.
Maybe you have spent years running.
Come home.
Maybe you have hidden your sin beneath religious language.
Repent.
Maybe you have confused church attendance with knowing Christ.
Seek Him.
Maybe you have fallen again.
Get up and turn toward Jesus.
Maybe shame keeps telling you that God could never forgive someone like you.
Look at the cross.
Grace is not permission to remain in sin.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness that leads us away from the grave and into a transformed life with Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of what is killing you.
And perhaps your first courageous act today is not conquering some visible giant.
Perhaps it is finally becoming honest before God.
“No more pretending.”
“No more hiding.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
If that is where your heart is right now, let your response become more than emotion.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer sees at midnight and realizes:
I am not fighting alone.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

But if the Gospel has strengthened you, sharing biblical truth can become one simple way of serving someone else. Someone scrolling through Facebook tonight may be silently standing before a giant nobody else can see.
Let them encounter hope.
Because giants have an irritating habit of returning after inspirational moments are over.
“The LORD is with us. Do not fear them.”
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is growing cold.
Invite the person who is questioning everything.
Invite the friend who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Invite even the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
Supporting Gospel work is a meaningful act of generosity when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory—not as a transaction for divine favor.
And there is more.
Deeper than a comment.
Deeper than a share.
He is calling you to Himself.
Because eventually every Facebook post disappears down a feed.
Every shirt wears out.
Every mug breaks.
Every book grows old.
Every human platform eventually disappears.
But Jesus Christ remains.
So when the giants rise tomorrow, remember Joshua.
Remember Caleb.
Remember the ten men who allowed what they saw to become greater in their hearts than what God had said.
And remember those devastating words:
“We were in our own eyes like grasshoppers.”
Do not let fear become your identity.
You may feel weak.
You may be wounded.
You may have failed.
You may still be trembling.
But if you belong to Christ, trembling does not mean abandoned.
The giant can be real.
The tears can be real.
The battle can be real.
And God can still be faithful.
Because perhaps somewhere tonight there is another frightened person staring at another impossible giant.
And perhaps the truth God used to strengthen you is exactly what they need to encounter next.
The giant may be standing in front of you—but it does not get to sit on God's throne.
